**Answer: Yes, $A_n \to A$ in operator norm.** In fact, compactness is not needed; the result holds for all bounded positive self-adjoint operators.

---

**Proof.**

We work on a Hilbert space $H$. Recall that for a bounded self-adjoint operator $T$ and a continuous function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, the continuous functional calculus gives an operator $f(T)$ satisfying
$$\|f(T)\| = \sup_{\lambda\in\sigma(T)} |f(\lambda)|. \tag{1}$$

We first establish a general lemma.

**Lemma (Norm-continuity of the functional calculus).** *Let $T_n, T$ be bounded self-adjoint operators on $H$ with $\|T_n - T\|\to 0$. If $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $\|f(T_n)-f(T)\|\to 0$.*

*Proof of Lemma.* Since $\|T_n-T\|\to 0$, we have $\|T_n\|\to\|T\|$, so there exist $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ and $M>0$ such that $\|T_n\|\le M$ and $\|T\|\le M$ for all $n\ge N_0$. By the spectral radius formula for self-adjoint operators, $\sigma(T_n)\cup\sigma(T)\subseteq[-M,M]$ for all $n\ge N_0$.

The function $f$ is continuous on the compact interval $[-M,M]$, hence uniformly continuous. By the Weierstrass approximation theorem, for any $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a polynomial $p$ such that
$$\sup_{t\in[-M,M]}|f(t)-p(t)|<\varepsilon.$$

For $n\ge N_0$, using (1) and $\sigma(T_n)\subseteq[-M,M]$:
$$\|f(T_n)-p(T_n)\|=\sup_{\lambda\in\sigma(T_n)}|f(\lambda)-p(\lambda)|\le\varepsilon,$$
and similarly $\|f(T)-p(T)\|\le\varepsilon$.

Since $p$ is a polynomial, say $p(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}c_k t^k$, the estimate
$$\|p(T_n)-p(T)\|\le\sum_{k=1}^{d}|c_k|\,\|T_n^k-T^k\|$$
together with $\|T_n^k-T^k\|\le\bigl(\|T_n\|^{k-1}+\|T_n\|^{k-2}\|T\|+\cdots+\|T\|^{k-1}\bigr)\|T_n-T\|\to 0$
shows $\|p(T_n)-p(T)\|\to 0$.

Combining via the triangle inequality:
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\|f(T_n)-f(T)\|\le\limsup_{n\to\infty}\|f(T_n)-p(T_n)\|+\lim_{n\to\infty}\|p(T_n)-p(T)\|+\|p(T)-f(T)\|\le 2\varepsilon.$$
Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, $\|f(T_n)-f(T)\|\to 0$. $\qquad\square$

---

**Application to the square root.**

Since each $Q_n$ and $Q$ is positive and self-adjoint (symmetric), its spectrum lies in $[0,\infty)$. Define
$$f(t)=\begin{cases}\sqrt{t}, & t\ge 0,\\ 0, & t<0.\end{cases}$$
This $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ (continuity at $0$ is clear since $f(t)\to 0$ as $t\to 0^+$ and $f(t)=0$ for $t<0$).

Because $\sigma(Q_n),\sigma(Q)\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and $f$ agrees with $\sqrt{\cdot}$ on $[0,\infty)$, the functional calculus gives
$$f(Q_n)=Q_n^{1/2}=A_n,\qquad f(Q)=Q^{1/2}=A.$$

The hypotheses give $Q_n\to Q$ in operator norm, with all operators self-adjoint. By the Lemma,
$$\|A_n-A\|=\|f(Q_n)-f(Q)\|\to 0.$$

Therefore $A_n\to A$ in operator norm. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Remark.** Compactness of $Q_n$ and $Q$ was not used; the conclusion holds for arbitrary bounded positive self-adjoint operators. (The only property of compact positive operators that is relevant is that $0\in\sigma(Q)$ whenever $\dim H=\infty$, which actually makes naive approaches via inverting $D\mapsto DA+AD$ fail — but the functional-calculus argument above bypasses this entirely.)
